notes: Garden Tracker bees reference pack: how-to-start guides, hive diseases and pests (with notifiable notes), pollinator flowers for the Bee Happy badge, and hive health labels. Text is in our own words at about a 3rd-grade reading level. Worldwide wording: no month names. Metric first. Facts checked against the cited extension pages. Link Bees lessons instead of repeating them. Bump version when this pack changes. v2 adds hive types, bee sources, mite methods, feeding types, and Honey Bee Health Coalition mite-count guidance. Short forms are written out at first use (nucleus colony (nuc), package of bees, honey boxes (supers), American and European foulbrood).

guides.blurb: Laws about keeping honey bees differ around the world.
body: Before you get bees, check your local rules. Some places need a permit. Some ask you to sign up your hives. Rules differ around the world, so ask your local bee group or farm office.
It is also wise to talk with close neighbors. Some people are allergic to bee stings.
If you later find a notifiable disease or pest, you may have to tell a bee inspector. Check those rules too, before you need them.

guides.blurb: Bee stings can be mild, or they can be a medical emergency.
body: Wear a veil and closed shoes when you work a hive. Use a smoker and a hive tool, and stand to the side of the entrance, not in the bees' flight path.
If you already know you are allergic to stings, talk to a doctor first. A doctor may give you emergency medicine to have on hand.
For a mild sting, ice can help. If breathing is hard, get emergency care at once. Do the same if the face or throat swells, or if a person feels faint.
lessons: A hive inspection, step by step

guides.blurb: A good spot keeps the bees healthier and is kinder to neighbors.
body: Place the hive where it gets morning sun and some afternoon shade. Shelter it from strong wind. Avoid a low, damp spot.
Set the flight path so bees do not cross a sidewalk, playground, or a neighbor's door. A fence can lift their flight path over people's heads.

guides.blurb: Many beginners start with a nucleus colony (nuc) or a package of bees, plus basic gear.
body: A nucleus colony (nuc) is a small starter hive. It often comes with a queen, workers, and a few frames of comb already built.
A package of bees (package) is a screened box of worker bees, with a queen in a cage. You install them in an empty hive and they must build comb.

Beginner kits often include a hive (many people start with a Langstroth hive, which is a stack of boxes with frames you can lift out, sometimes already fitted with foundation), a veil, gloves, a smoker, and a hive tool. Learn how your hive’s frames and boxes fit before the bees arrive. Honey is stored in honey boxes (supers) stacked above the brood box, where the queen lays eggs.

diseases.signs: Tiny mites on bees or brood. A high mite count on a mite wash. A weak hive, deformed wings, or a sudden drop in bees can be later signs.
diseases.what: Varroa mites feed on honey bees and their brood and can spread viruses. You cannot wipe them out for good, but you can keep numbers low if you test often and act in time. Follow the label on any treatment.
lessons: Varroa mites and how to count them

diseases.notifiableNote: In many places, foulbrood must be reported. Tell the local bee inspector if you know or even suspect it. Do not try to treat it yourself. Do not move bees, comb, honey, or gear from that hive until you are told what to do.
diseases.signs: A spotty brood pattern. Caps may look sunken or have holes. Remains may be brown or greasy, with a bad smell. In American foulbrood, the remains may pull out like a brown, sticky thread. Dried scales can stick to the cell.
diseases.what: American foulbrood is a serious brood disease caused by germs. Sick larvae die in the cells. Check your local rules. A bee inspector can tell you what to do next.

diseases.notifiableNote: In many places, foulbrood must be reported. Tell the local bee inspector if you know or even suspect it. Check your local rules before you treat or move anything.
diseases.signs: A spotty brood pattern and dead or discolored larvae in open cells. There may be a sour smell. Caps may look sunken. It can look a bit like American foulbrood, so do not guess — get advice.
diseases.what: European foulbrood is also a serious brood disease caused by germs. Because it can be mixed up with American foulbrood, report a suspected case if your local rules say you must, and ask an inspector or a local bee group for help.

diseases.notifiableNote: In some countries this beetle is notifiable, and in some it is not yet present. If you think you have found it, check your local rules and report it if you must.
diseases.signs: Small, dark beetles that hide in cracks and run on the comb. Their larvae may tunnel through comb and spoil brood and stores.
diseases.what: Small hive beetles can wreck weak hives and stored comb. Keep colonies strong and store spare comb clean and protected. Ask a local bee group what works where you live.

diseases.signs: Silky tunnels, webbing, and chewed comb, especially in weak hives or in empty comb you have taken off the hive.
diseases.what: Wax moths lay eggs on comb. The larvae eat wax and can ruin stored frames. Store spare comb clean, dry, and protected. Do not use ordinary moth balls on bee gear, because they can harm bees.

diseases.notifiableNote: In some regions, the yellow-legged hornet is a serious threat and must be reported. Learn which pests are a problem in your area, and which ones you must report.
diseases.signs: Hornets hunting honey bees at the entrance, or many bees suddenly missing.
diseases.what: Some hornets hunt honey bees. Learn which pests are a problem where you live, and which ones you must report.

health.hint: Plenty of bees, brood, and stores.
The hive looks healthy enough for now.
Fewer bees than you would like, or low stores.
You did not see the queen. That does not always mean she is gone.
Something worries you — pests, disease signs, or a sudden change.
Something needs a closer look soon, such as queen cells or a rising mite count.
Act soon — for example a high mite count, or no eggs and no queen seen.

flowers.name: Sweet alyssum
flowers.note: Tiny flowers that feed bees and hover flies over a long bloom.

flowers.name: Marigold
flowers.note: Easy flowers that bees and other helpful insects visit.

flowers.name: Nasturtium
flowers.note: Bright flowers bees visit; you can eat the leaves and blooms too.

flowers.name: Borage
flowers.note: Blue, starry flowers that bees love. It often sows itself.

flowers.name: Lavender
flowers.note: A dry-soil shrub whose blooms are a favorite of bees.

flowers.name: Bee balm (monarda)
flowers.note: Spiky blooms that bees and hummingbirds visit.

flowers.name: Zinnia
flowers.note: Single-flowered kinds are easier for bees than very tight pompoms.

flowers.name: Cosmos
flowers.note: Open, daisy-like flowers that are easy for bees to use.

flowers.name: Calendula
flowers.note: Cool-season blooms that feed bees and can be used in the kitchen.

flowers.name: Buckwheat
flowers.note: A fast cover crop whose flowers give bees a short, rich feast.

flowers.name: Clover
flowers.note: A living mulch and cover crop that bees work when it blooms.

flowers.name: Phacelia
flowers.note: A cover-crop flower that many bees visit.

flowers.name: Coneflower
flowers.note: A hardy perennial with open flowers and seed heads birds use later.

Population increase (the colony is building up)

Sugar syrup 2:1 (twice as much sugar as water)

miteGuide.sampleNote: A usual sample is about 300 adult bees, which is about 120 ml (½ cup) of lightly packed bees. Count the real number if you can.
miteGuide.text: The Honey Bee Health Coalition (9th edition, June 2026) uses conservative estimates: promptly control mites at 1 or more mites per 100 adult bees when the colony is dormant or building up, and at 2 or more per 100 bees at the peak or when the population is decreasing. These levels can vary by region. An alcohol or soap wash is the more reliable test. A powdered-sugar roll is more prone to error. A sticky board is a whole-hive check, not a count per 100 bees. Always follow the label on any treatment. The app will not tell you how much product to use.
